slides.title: The report needs values, not the storage plan
keyPoints: Visit readings in insertion order
Allow two reports to stop at different positions
Keep the collection representation private
slides.narration: A measurement log contains four and nine. One report needs their sum; another is still examining the first reading. We could give both reports the whole vector. That is easy today, but each report could start depending on indexing, contiguous storage, or the ability to change the vector. If the log later uses chunks, those assumptions become obstacles. The needed behavior is smaller: ask whether traversal is finished, read one value, and advance. An iterator is a separate object that holds this traversal position. The chapter calls its teaching interface Cursor. First we will see why an ordinary vector loop is enough until storage independence becomes a real requirement.

question.prompt: Which information belongs to the report cursor rather than the collection itself?
question.answer: The report’s current traversal position. Different reports need independent positions over the same values.

slides.title: Use the existing container when its contract fits
keyPoints: Range-based for already traverses a vector
The colon means: take each element from this range
An int loop variable holds a copied reading
slides.narration: The shortest reasonable report uses a vector and a range-based for loop. In for followed by int value, a colon, and readings, the colon separates the element declaration from the range being visited. Each integer is copied into value, then added to total. The collection itself does not change. The result is thirteen. This is already a sound use of iteration supplied by the standard library; writing a custom Cursor would not improve this tiny program. Our later wrapper is justified by a different public contract: reports should not know that the storage is a vector, and mutation should have an explicit checked policy. Keep the baseline as a reference when judging that added complexity.

question.prompt: Does assigning a new number to value change the stored reading here?

slides.title: A single position cannot serve independent readers
keyPoints: One shared index couples unrelated reports
A copied position can move independently
Traversal state should travel with the traversal
slides.narration: Imagine placing a current_index member directly in the measurement log and letting every report use it. The first report advances, and the second unexpectedly starts at nine instead of four. The data did not change; the reports accidentally shared their progress. That is the pressure for a separate position object. Each Cursor contains its own index while borrowing the same Readings owner. Copying a cursor copies the position, so advancing the copy leaves the original alone. This does not mean the data was copied. The design separates two kinds of state: values owned by the collection and progress owned by each traversal. That separation lets reports compose without resetting one another.
actions: Trace one cursor to nine while leaving its copy at four.

question.prompt: If two cursors share the collection, must they also share the index?
question.answer: No. Each cursor stores its own index. Sharing the owner does not require sharing traversal progress.

slides.title: An in-range index can still belong to stale work
keyPoints: Bounds checking protects an element access
A generation check protects the traversal contract
Appending can invalidate a cursor without changing its index
slides.narration: This controlled model keeps a copied index rather than a standard vector iterator, so no invalid iterator is dereferenced. Before the append, index zero refers to four and the saved generation is two. After adding twelve, index zero is still within bounds and at still returns four. Yet the saved generation no longer matches. Under the chapter's chosen policy, the old traversal is stale because any successful append ends it. A bound check alone cannot enforce that rule. The word stale means an old view of a changed collection, not necessarily a missing element. Later we place the version comparison inside every public cursor operation so callers cannot forget it.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Visit readings in insertion order and support independent positions.
Make empty/end behavior explicit.
Reject cursor operations after a successful append.
slides.narration:
A checked cursor over a readings log. Cursor stores only a borrowed owner, saved version, and index. Readings keeps its representation private and refuses copying or moving that could complicate its identity. Values are copied out.

Visit readings in insertion order and support independent positions. Make empty/end behavior explicit. Reject cursor operations after a successful append.

The owner must remain alive and in place while a cursor is used. A live cursor index is at most the number of readings. A version mismatch is rejected before data access. An end position is never read as an element. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. Expose a vector const_iterator if the public contract can depend on vector rules. Own a snapshot if scans must survive later edits or owner destruction. A snapshot gives stability in exchange for copying and storage costs.

comparisons.label: Chosen design
comparisons.text: Cursor stores only a borrowed owner, saved version, and index. Readings keeps its representation private and refuses copying or moving that could complicate its identity. Values are copied out.

comparisons.label: A reasonable alternative
comparisons.text: Expose a vector const_iterator if the public contract can depend on vector rules. Own a snapshot if scans must survive later edits or owner destruction. A snapshot gives stability in exchange for copying and storage costs.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Iterator implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: The owner must remain alive and in place while a cursor is used. A live cursor index is at most the number of readings. A version mismatch is rejected before data access. An end position is never read as an element.

slides.title: The problem: callers need readings, not storage details
keyPoints: A measurement log stores a sequence of integer readings.
Giving every caller a reference to the internal vector exposes more than traversal.
slides.narration:
A measurement log stores a sequence of integer readings. A report must visit the readings in insertion order and compute their total. The simplest loop uses a vector directly, and that is often the best answer when the vector is already part of the public design. The new constraint is that reports should not depend on the storage layout. The log may later use chunks, a file cache, or a filtered view. Reports also need independent positions: one view may be examining the first reading while another has reached the second.

Giving every caller a reference to the internal vector exposes more than traversal. Callers can start depending on contiguous memory, indexing, and mutation details. Copying the entire vector into every report hides storage but can waste memory when readings are numerous. We need a small object that remembers a position and provides the next value without handing over the container. That object is an iterator. The teaching implementation calls it Cursor to emphasize its explicit done, read, and next operations.

question.prompt: Two readers walk the same collection at different speeds. What state must remain separate?
question.answer: Each reader needs its own traversal position. They may share the stored readings, but advancing one reader must not advance the other. Changes to the collection need a separate invalidation rule.

slides.title: Separate a collection from a position within it
keyPoints: Readings owns its vector and a version number.
The nested class declaration places Cursor inside Readings as part of its interface.
slides.narration:
Readings owns its vector and a version number. Cursor borrows the Readings object, stores the version seen at creation, and starts its own index at zero. The collection therefore holds data while each cursor holds traversal state. Copying a cursor copies its position and saved version but still refers to the same owner. Advancing the copy does not advance the original. In the example, one cursor moves to nine while an independent copy still reads four.

The nested class declaration places Cursor inside Readings as part of its interface. A nested class can access the enclosing class private members through an object; it does not carry an implicit enclosing object by magic. owner_ provides that actual object. const Readings& prevents the cursor from modifying the owner through that reference. It does not prevent other code from calling append on the original non-const collection. That distinction is why a read-only reference does not make a changing collection safe by itself.

slides.title: An end position exists, but it is not an element
keyPoints: For two readings, legal traversal positions are index zero, index one, and index two as the end marker.
The report loop checks !scan.done before calling read.
slides.narration:
For two readings, legal traversal positions are index zero, index one, and index two as the end marker. done reports true at index two. There is no third reading to return. read calls vector.at, which checks the bound and throws std::out_of_range when asked for the end element. next also rejects an attempt to step beyond end. Empty collections begin at end, so the same loop works without a special branch in the report.

The report loop checks !scan.done before calling read. The exclamation mark means not: it enters the body only while the cursor is not at end. After reading, scan.next advances one position. read returns int by value, so the report receives an independent copy. An element reference could avoid copying a large object, but that reference would introduce its own invalidation and lifetime rules. A copied integer keeps this first traversal interface honest and small. The cursor still borrows the collection and must not outlive it.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch15.json → A changed collection makes old cursors stale
slides.title: A changed collection makes old cursors stale
keyPoints: Invalidation means that an operation has ended a cursor validity under its documented rules.
A stale cursor is different from a cursor at end.
slides.narration:
Invalidation means that an operation has ended a cursor validity under its documented rules. This implementation chooses a strict policy: every successful append invalidates every existing cursor, even if the vector happened to have spare capacity. append first checks that the version counter can be increased without wrapping, then appends the value, then increases the version. If vector growth fails, neither the collection contents nor the version is committed by this append of an integer. A cursor compares its captured version with the current version before done, read, or next proceeds.

A stale cursor is different from a cursor at end. End is a valid position in an unchanged collection. Stale means the view no longer matches the collection generation, even if its numeric index remains within bounds. Merely using at would detect a bad index but would not detect a changed traversal contract. The program checks this difference by creating a cursor, appending twelve, and rejecting use of the old cursor. Version exhaustion is rejected instead of wrapping to an old number that might make a stale cursor look current.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch15.json → A safety check cannot bring a dead owner back
slides.title: A safety check cannot bring a dead owner back
keyPoints: The version check reads owner_.stamp_.
Alternative designs make different promises.
slides.narration:
The version check reads owner_.stamp_. If the Readings object has already been destroyed, even that first read would use a dangling reference. The check therefore protects against documented mutation while the owner is alive; it is not a general lifetime detector. main declares the collection first and all cursors later, so the collection outlives them. Copy and assignment of Readings are deleted in this example, and it has no implicit move operation. Its identity stays fixed while cursors borrow it.

Alternative designs make different promises. A snapshot cursor could own a copy of the values, remain valid after append, and cost more memory. A cursor holding shared ownership of an immutable collection can extend lifetime without copying its data. Standard-library containers already supply carefully specified iterators; use them when their contracts fit. This Cursor deliberately does not claim to model a standard C++ iterator category: it lacks operator*, operator++, comparison, and the related type information. It teaches the separation of traversal state from storage without pretending to work with every standard algorithm.

slides.title: Choose traversal features from the reporting problem
keyPoints: A forward scan is enough for the total.
The primary tests establish behavior for a small deterministic collection, an empty collection, independent positions, end access, end advancement, and stale access.
slides.narration:
A forward scan is enough for the total. The lab introduces a real new need: show the newest readings first. Its reverse cursor stores the number of elements still available and reads the element at remaining minus one. It checks for zero before subtracting, because size_t is unsigned and zero minus one would wrap to a huge value. Forward and reverse cursors follow the same version policy, so a caller does not need to guess which mutation rules apply.

The primary tests establish behavior for a small deterministic collection, an empty collection, independent positions, end access, end advancement, and stale access. They do not prove thread safety. Concurrent append and read without synchronization can create a data race; a version integer is not a lock. A real reporting subsystem should either prevent concurrent edits during a scan, take a stable snapshot, or define synchronization around both data and cursor checks. The traversal interface makes that choice easier to review, but cannot make it disappear.

question.prompt: Why use remaining minus one for reverse read?
question.answer: remaining counts unread elements. For a nonempty view, the next reverse index is one less than that count; checking empty first prevents unsigned underflow.

slides.title: A nested type still needs an actual owner
keyPoints: Readings owns values_ and stamp_
Cursor stores owner_, stamp_, and index_
const restricts this access path; it does not freeze the owner
slides.narration: Cursor is declared inside Readings, which makes it a nested class. That placement grants access to the enclosing class's private members, but it does not magically provide a particular Readings object. The owner_ reference supplies that object. The const in const Readings& prevents the cursor from modifying the owner through this reference. It does not stop other code from calling append on a non-const Readings. Cursor also stores the generation it saw at creation and its own index. The compiler checks access and const rules when building the program. It cannot know whether someone will append later, so comparing generations is a runtime responsibility.
actions: Separate owner identity, saved generation, and current index on the board.

question.prompt: Can another reference append while a cursor has a const Readings&?
question.answer: Yes. const restricts modification through that reference. It does not make the underlying object immutable to every other access path.

slides.title: End is a position, not a hidden last element
keyPoints: Two readings have positions 0, 1, and end at 2
done is true at end
read and next reject operations past their contract
slides.narration: With two readings, zero and one select values. Two is the valid end position and selects no value. This extra position lets a loop stop without special knowledge of the last element. An empty collection starts at end immediately. The chapter's loop tests not done before reading, then advances once. The exclamation mark negates the boolean result: enter only while not finished. read uses at, so reading end throws instead of accessing unchecked memory. next rejects another advance from end. These are explicit contracts of the teaching Cursor, not a claim that every library iterator permits the same operations or throws the same errors.
actions: Trace empty and two-element loops using the same control flow.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch15.json → An end position exists, but it is not an element

question.prompt: For an empty Readings, may read be called after done returns true?
question.answer: No. End is a valid traversal position but contains no readable value.

slides.title: Commit the collection change before the new version
keyPoints: Every successful append invalidates all old cursors
Increase stamp_ after push_back succeeds
Reject counter exhaustion instead of wrapping
slides.narration: The generation records successful collection changes. append first checks whether increasing the counter would exhaust its range. It then adds the integer to the vector, and only after success increases stamp_. If allocating more vector storage fails for this integer append, the contents and generation remain as they were. Incrementing first could invalidate cursors even though no append took place. Letting the counter wrap creates the opposite risk: an ancient cursor could accidentally match a repeated number. The strict policy does not depend on vector capacity. Even an append that uses spare memory makes all old cursors stale. That predictable rule is easier to explain than an accidental dependency on allocation behavior.
actions: Ask learners to distinguish the wrapper’s contract from vector’s own iterator rules.

question.prompt: Should reserving spare capacity keep an old chapter Cursor valid after append?
question.answer: No. This Cursor invalidates on every successful append, regardless of whether vector storage moves.

slides.title: A version number cannot resurrect an owner
keyPoints: Checking stamp_ itself reads the borrowed owner
Readings must outlive its cursors
A generation counter is not a synchronization lock
slides.narration: validate compares two numbers, but one number lives inside owner_. If that object has died, even performing the safety check is already invalid. The version mechanism therefore checks mutation while the owner is alive; it is not a lifetime detector. In main, Readings is declared before the cursors so its lifetime extends beyond theirs. The class also rejects copying and assignment, which keeps its identity simple and suppresses an implicit move in this design. None of this makes concurrent reads and appends safe. Two threads still need a shared synchronization rule around the data and checks. A snapshot or immutable shared owner changes these guarantees, but also changes cost and ownership.
actions: Identify the first owner access in validate, not just the later element read.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch15.json → A safety check cannot bring a dead owner back

question.prompt: Can validate safely detect that a borrowed owner has been destroyed?
question.answer: No. It must access the owner to read the version. The owner’s lifetime must already be guaranteed.

slides.title: Reverse traversal needs a careful zero boundary
keyPoints: remaining_ counts unread elements
Read remaining_ minus one only after checking zero
Preserve the same generation and owner rules
slides.narration: The reverse extension answers a new reporting need: show the newest reading first. It stores how many elements remain. With three readings, remaining is three, so the first index is two; next reduces the count to two. At zero there is no next index to compute. size_t is unsigned, so zero minus one wraps to a very large value instead of becoming a useful negative index. The source therefore checks done before subtracting. This design is not just the forward loop written backward. Its state meaning differs, while lifetime, stale-generation checking, and end rejection stay consistent. Keeping those shared rules makes future reporting features easier to test and explain.
actions: Trace remaining values 3, 2, 1, 0 beside indices 2, 1, 0.

question.prompt: Why must the reverse cursor check remaining_ before subtracting one?
question.answer: remaining_ uses an unsigned type. Subtracting one from zero wraps and does not represent a valid previous element.

slides.title: Keep these rules when the program grows
keyPoints: A cursor owns its position, not necessarily its collection.
End is a valid position with no readable element.
Bounds and generation are separate checks.
Read-only access does not freeze other access paths.
Custom traversal interfaces should not claim standard-iterator compatibility without meeting its requirements.
slides.narration:
A cursor owns its position, not necessarily its collection. End is a valid position with no readable element. Bounds and generation are separate checks. Read-only access does not freeze other access paths. Custom traversal interfaces should not claim standard-iterator compatibility without meeting its requirements.

Callers depend on a traversal contract instead of vector storage. Future representation changes must preserve order, lifetime, and invalidation semantics or deliberately revise that contract.

question.prompt: Explain Iterator without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Cursor stores only a borrowed owner, saved version, and index. Readings keeps its representation private and refuses copying or moving that could complicate its identity. Values are copied out. Expose a vector const_iterator if the public contract can depend on vector rules. Own a snapshot if scans must survive later edits or owner destruction. A snapshot gives stability in exchange for copying and storage costs.

slides.title: Custom Cursor or standard iterator?
keyPoints: Use standard iterators when their contracts already fit
Choose a snapshot when readers need stable old data
Do not claim algorithm compatibility that is not implemented
slides.narration: The custom Cursor teaches independent traversal and a deliberately checked mutation policy. It does not implement the standard iterator operations, comparisons, and type information expected by ordinary standard-library algorithms. Naming something an iterator does not make it usable by every algorithm. If a vector is already the intended public representation, its existing iterators are usually the simpler choice. If a report must survive later appends, a copied snapshot may be more useful than rejecting stale access, at the cost of copied data. Shared immutable storage can reduce copying while extending lifetime. Compare these options by the report's consistency and ownership needs before judging their syntax.
actions: Ask which report requirement justifies snapshot cost.

question.prompt: Can this Cursor be passed directly to every algorithm that accepts standard iterators?
question.answer: No. It exposes done/read/next rather than the full required standard iterator interface and semantics.

slides.title: Three failures need three different tests
keyPoints: End access: no value exists at this position
Stale access: the generation changed
Dangling owner: the lifetime promise was broken
slides.narration: Do not collapse every traversal failure into out of range. At end, the owner is alive and unchanged, but no element occupies the current position. A stale cursor may still have index zero, yet its generation contract has ended. A dangling cursor has no valid owner to inspect and must be prevented by design, not demonstrated by executing undefined behavior. The chapter tests empty input, independent positions, end reads, end advancement, and mutation rejection. When adding reverse traversal, repeat the contract tests for that direction rather than checking only the printed reverse order. A sequence that prints twelve, nine, four can still mishandle empty input or wrap after the last element.
actions: Ask learners to name a safe test for each documented condition.

question.prompt: Which test distinguishes a stale cursor from ordinary end access?
question.answer: Create a cursor at a valid element, append successfully, then require the old cursor operation to reject the generation mismatch.

slides.title: Describe the boundary between data and travel
keyPoints: The collection owns readings
Each cursor owns a position and a validity view
The contract says how mutation ends that view
slides.narration: Explain Iterator without starting from pointer syntax. A collection keeps values. A small separate object remembers where one caller is in those values and provides a limited way to visit them. Two callers can move independently without seeing the collection's internal layout. Then explain the chapter's additional rules: append ends existing views, end is not an element, and the owner must remain alive. Transfer this to paged records from a file cache. A cursor could remember a page and offset, but the report could still ask for the next reading. Storage independence is useful only if the public traversal contract remains clear about failures, freshness, and cost.
actions: Have learners explain a chunked-storage change without exposing vector operations.

question.prompt: What can change behind a stable traversal interface, and what must remain explicit?
question.answer: Storage layout can change. Ordering, validity after mutation, lifetime, failure behavior, and performance assumptions still need a clear contract.

graph.title: Two cursor positions, one owner
graph.caption: Only the collection-to-elements edge means ownership. Both cursor dependencies borrow the same Readings object, but each cursor has its own index and version value. Copying a cursor does not copy the readings or create shared ownership. The two iterator nodes are distinct Cursor instances. They share the collection, not their traversal positions.
